Computational Ranking of Surface Micro-Texture Geometries for Drag Reduction

Which surface texture cuts the most drag?

Kanav Thonda, Rouse High School, Leander, Texas
Manuscript prepared 23 August 2026 · 67 geometries · 5 flow speeds · 2 test bodies · 13 validation benchmarks

Explore the results Read the paper Download the data

Abstract

The full manuscript, all 670 data rows and the complete handoff document are embedded in this page and downloadable below.

Scope and honesty note. This is a reduced-order semi-empirical model calibrated against published experiments, not a first-principles CFD campaign and not a wind-tunnel measurement. Its contribution is the systematic cross-class, cross-Reynolds, cross-body comparison under one consistent framework with propagated uncertainty. Of the 13 validation benchmarks, only 3 are genuinely independent predictions the model was never fitted to; the rest confirm that published correlations were implemented and calibrated correctly.

Key findings

Every value below is computed from the embedded dataset, not typed in.

Best geometry overall
B-HEX-d2.0-r0.1
52.77% ± 4.1 pp net drag reduction on the sphere at 50 m/s, drag coefficient 0.490 → 0.232. Best plate result: A-BLAD-s200-h100 at 9.51%.
Best geometry class
Riblets on the plate,
dimples on the sphere
The ranking reverses with the dominant drag component. Plate class means: riblet +1.09%, dimple -6.25%. Sphere: dimple +7.96%, riblet +1.72%.
Optimal riblet spacing
s⁺ = 15.5–18.1
Emergent, not fitted — the model is parameterised on the groove scale l_g⁺, which collapses to 10.70–10.72 across all four profiles. Operating in-band is worth 2.70 pp.
Where texture matters most
50 m/s
Largest achievable reduction of any geometry (52.8%, sphere). On the friction-dominated plate the peak comes earlier, at 20 m/s (9.51%), then falls as riblets overshoot their optimal s⁺.

Interactive drag reduction explorer

Pick a texture class, a specific variant, a test body and a flow speed. The bar chart compares the smooth baseline against the textured surface; the cross-section below is drawn to scale from the selected geometry's actual dimensions, with the viscous sublayer thickness at that speed overlaid.

Flat plate is compared on skin-friction coefficient Cᶠ; the sphere is compared on total drag coefficient C_d, because its drag is dominated by pressure rather than friction.
--

Geometry comparison tool

Select up to five geometries to overlay their drag reduction against flow speed. Curves that cross the zero line change from helping to hurting as speed rises — the clearest demonstration that there is no single best texture.

Figures

All eight figures as scalable vector graphics. Figure 6 is presented separately in the next section.

Figure 1

Top 20 geometries by net drag reduction

Horizontal bars with propagated 1-sigma uncertainty. Bars whose intervals overlap the leader are flagged as statistical ties rather than ranked against it.
Figure 2

Drag reduction versus flow speed

Top plate and sphere geometries. Several curves cross zero - the best low-speed geometry is not the best high-speed geometry.
Figure 3

Riblet performance map: spacing x height

The full 4x4 V-groove grid at every speed, no empty cells. Categorical axes are rendered as uniform bins although the underlying values are not evenly spaced.
Figure 4

Drag reduction versus riblet spacing in wall units

The shaded band is the published s+ = 10-20 optimum. The model was parameterised on the groove scale l_g+, so landing inside this band is an emergent result.
Figure 5

Dimple performance map: diameter x depth ratio

Deep dimples are strongly net-negative on the plate: the form-drag penalty scales with the square of depth ratio while the friction credit does not.
Figure 7

Pareto fronts: performance versus manufacturability

Left: drag reduction against the smallest feature that must be fabricated. Right: against a composite process-difficulty index.
Figure 8

Distribution of drag reduction by geometry class

The class-level reversal between plate and sphere is visible as a swap in the relative position of the riblet and dimple boxes.

Flow physics

Figure 6 is built from computed velocity profiles rather than drawn as an illustration, so the laminar-versus-turbulent contrast and the near-wall geometry are quantitatively correct and to scale.

Figure 6

Boundary-layer flow visualisation

Computed Blasius and Spalding profiles with near-wall detail for smooth, riblet and dimple surfaces, drawn to scale. Not a schematic.
Blasius vs SpaldingThe laminar Blasius profile and the turbulent Spalding law-of-the-wall profile are both solved numerically at U = 10 m/s, giving boundary-layer thicknesses of 1.98 mm and 2.18 mm respectively.
Viscous sublayerAt 10 m/s the friction velocity is 0.63 m/s and the viscous length scale is 24.8 µm, so the sublayer is about 124 µm thick. Riblets only work if they sit inside it.
Why riblets win hereGrooves lift the cross-flow vortices away from the wall and restrict spanwise motion, cutting turbulent momentum transfer without adding meaningful wetted area.
Why dimples lose hereOn an attached flat-plate flow a dimple adds a form-drag penalty scaling with the square of depth ratio, while its friction credit does not scale the same way — so the net effect turns negative quickly.
Drag per unit areaAt 10 m/s the computed load is 0.469 Pa smooth, 0.444 Pa for the riblet surface (5.3% lower) and 0.467 Pa for the dimpled surface (0.5% lower).
Known inconsistencyThe 0.37·L·Re-0.2 correlation gives 4.05 mm for the turbulent thickness against 2.18 mm from the profile. Both are extrapolated below their validated Reynolds range; the figure uses the profile-derived value and the paper says so.

Computational Ranking of Surface Micro-Texture Geometries for Aerodynamic Drag Reduction Across Flow Regimes
Kanav Thonda, Rouse High School, Leander, Texas · manuscript prepared 23 August 2026.

Reduced-order semi-empirical model composed from published peer-reviewed correlations. 670 cases, 13 validation benchmarks (13 passed, maximum absolute point error 2.42%). Air at 25 °C, ρ = 1.184 kg/m³. Flat plate L = 0.1 m assumed tripped to a turbulent boundary layer; sphere D = 42.7 mm.

This page is a single self-contained HTML file. Chart.js and the Inter typeface are loaded from public CDNs; every other asset, including all eight figures, the full dataset, the manuscript and the handoff document, is embedded.
